Question: How does a heterozygous single nucleotide substitution appear on a chromatogram?

Options:
A. One peak twice the height of those around it
B. Three peaks of equal height at the same position
C. Two peaks in the same position, one twice the height of the other
D. Two peaks of equal height at the same position

Thought: Let me think about what a heterozygous single nucleotide substitution means. In a heterozygous state, an individual has two different alleles at a specific locus. In DNA sequencing, when we look at a chromatogram (the graphical representation of DNA sequencing results), each nucleotide position typically shows a colored peak representing the base at that position.

For a heterozygous SNP (Single Nucleotide Polymorphism), the individual has two different nucleotides at the same position (one on each chromosome). When sequencing DNA from this individual, both nucleotides will be detected at that position.

On a chromatogram, this would appear as two different colored peaks at the same position - one for each nucleotide variant. Since the two alleles are typically present in equal amounts, the peaks would be of approximately equal height.

Looking at the options:
A. One peak twice the height - This would indicate a homozygous position, not heterozygous
B. Three peaks of equal height - This doesn't make sense for a single nucleotide position
C. Two peaks, one twice the height - This would suggest unequal representation of alleles, not typical for simple heterozygosity
D. Two peaks of equal height at the same position - This correctly describes how a heterozygous SNP appears on a chromatogram
Final Answer: [ANSWER]D[/ANSWER]
